rv.q: There is some fun to be had — a little — but this also scrambles the rules and bifurcates the show.

There's a strong musical somewhere in 'Leap of Faith,' which stars a soulful Raul Esparza and has some of Alan Menken's best songs. But what opened Thursday at The St. James Theatre is sometimes confusing in its tone.
But despite Raul Esparza's hard-working lead performance and some rousing gospel numbers from Alan Menken and Glenn Slater, the story remains stubbornly unappealing.
Despite the star power of Raul Esparza and a slick production, this musical about a con-man evangelist never finds its spiritual center or comic groove.
The show feels as if it were assembled by a committee of focus groups.
The show is well-intentioned but fatally confused about what it wants to say.
But the show shouldn't feel that way, too.

Want to make a ton of money? Peddle God to fools. Want to lose a ton of money? Invest in a Broadway turkey. You can’t have it both ways. It’s perfectly fine—even desirable—if your religion is crude and nonsensical, but a show as bland and confused as Leap of Faith is not going to make rich men of its producers (among whom are actual church leaders).
“Leap of Faith” is this season’s black hole of musical comedy, sucking the energy out of anyone who gets near it.
But there's a second-hand quality to the show that's hard to escape and not because it's based on a movie.
If the show offers any real revelation, it's that the playwriting does, too.
If only the show itself had enough faith to leap in one direction.
Esparza’s not a miracle worker; he can’t save the show.
Besides being a busy borrower, the derivative musical – its book is by Janus Cercone and Warren Leight, with direction by Christopher Ashley – leans heavily on clichés.

You know you're in trouble at 'Leap of Faith' even before the show starts, when actors pretending to be revivalists distribute what are supposed to be dollar bills to the audience, so we will have something to put in the collection basket when it's passed.

cn.t: Critics find "Leap of Faith" a confused, formulaic musical that wastes Raul Esparza's talent and Alan Menken's score, never finding its spiritual center or comic groove despite a slick production.

vs.sum: The St. James Theatre offers good sightlines for most seats, though the lack of a solid rake can be an issue if someone tall sits in front of you. The sound quality is generally good, but the tight legroom can be uncomfortable for taller patrons. The theater's ambiance is enhanced by its historic and grand interior, while facilities are average with standard amenities.

acc.note: No steps from sidewalk to Orchestra. No elevator. Mezzanine up 29 steps, Balcony up 76 steps.
